title: Unit 6b: Atmospheric Heat, Energy, Motion & Global Circulation
sub: Reading: pages 83–94  ·  20 points  ·  15 minutes  ·  Closed book
instructions: Answer every question. For multiple choice, circle the single best answer. Write short answers in complete sentences.

choices: how fast the atoms in a material vibrate
the amount of water vapor in the air
how well a surface reflects light
the air pressure at a given altitude
questions.why: p. 83 — a surface with high albedo reflects a large percentage of the light that hits it. A snowfield is the book’s example.

questions.stem: Latent heat is the heat taken in or released when a substance
questions.why: p. 84 — and while a substance is changing state its temperature does not change; all the energy goes into the change of state itself.

questions.stem: Water has a very high specific heat. This means that
choices: it takes a great deal of energy to change the temperature of water
water reflects almost all the light that strikes it
water heats up faster than asphalt in sunlight
questions.why: p. 85 — this is why a puddle stays cooler than an asphalt parking lot receiving the very same sunlight, and why oceans moderate coastal temperatures.

questions.stem: In the three-cell model, the Hadley cell is the convection cell found between
questions.why: p. 91 — the Ferrel cell runs from about 30° to 50–60°, and the Polar cell from about 50–60° to the pole.

questions.stem: Surface winds in the Hadley cell of the Northern Hemisphere blow from the northeast toward the southwest. These are called
questions.why: p. 92 — named because in the age of sailing ships they were reliable for trade. The deflection to the right is the Coriolis effect.

questions.stem: Chinook winds are warm and dry on the leeward side of a mountain range because
choices: the leeward side receives more direct sunlight
air that rose, cooled, and dropped its precipitation on the windward side then descends and warms
cold ocean air is drawn inland over the range
the mountains block the jet stream
questions.why: p. 89 — the same descending, drying air produces the rain shadow effect, which the text credits with creating many of the world’s deserts.

questions.stem: Wind belts are named for the direction the winds are blowing toward.
questions.why: They are named for the direction the winds come from. The westerlies blow from the west toward the east. (p. 93)

questions.stem: A jet stream forms where there is a large temperature difference between two air masses.
questions.why: p. 93 — a jet stream is a fast-flowing river of air at the boundary between troposphere and stratosphere. The polar jet stream is the world’s most powerful because the temperature contrast at the polar front is the sharpest.

questions.stem: Explain the difference between heat and temperature. Then say which has the higher temperature and which contains more heat: a candle flame, or a bathtub full of hot water.
questions.answer: Temperature measures how fast a material’s atoms are vibrating; heat measures the material’s total energy. The candle flame has the higher temperature; the bathtub contains far more heat.
questions.rubric: 1 pt temperature = speed of atomic vibration. 1 pt heat = total energy of the material. 1 pt for the comparison: the flame is hotter but its hot region is very small, while the bathtub is cooler but holds vastly more vibrating atoms and therefore greater total energy. (pp. 84–85)

questions.stem: Name the three convection cells of the three-cell model in one hemisphere, and give the approximate latitude range of each.
questions.answer: Hadley cell (0°–30°), Ferrel cell (30° to 50–60°), and Polar cell (50–60° to the pole).
questions.rubric: 1 pt per cell, requiring both the name and a roughly correct range. Accept 60° as the boundary between Ferrel and Polar. Bonus context, not required for credit: adjacent cells share their rising and descending limbs, the Southern Hemisphere mirrors these three, and the junction of the Ferrel and Polar cells is the polar front, where the polar jet stream is found. (pp. 91–93)
